## Bottom line

The craft here is good — better than most of what crosses this desk. The person who wrote this has actually looked at European transaction data: the consent-asymmetry point, the processor-confusion warning, the fixed-cohort YoY discipline, and the refusal to use panel share as market share are all things people learn the hard way. The methodology section is over-engineered but not naive.

The problem is that the plan never does the arithmetic that determines whether any of it is worth doing, and it has a structural contradiction at the top that dissolves the project either way. As scoped — 13 weeks, 700 candidates, 200 features — I would not fund this. I would fund a five-week gated feasibility study with three hard stops, described at the end.

---

## The three things that kill it

**1. The legal gate contains its own refutation.** Section 2 says most European transaction contracts prohibit re-identification, and that "the practical resolution is usually commercial: ask the vendor to sell a named financial-counterparty feed." If the vendor will sell that feed, the entire modelling project is unnecessary — you buy the answer for less than thirteen analyst-weeks. If the vendor won't sell it, that refusal is almost certainly the reason the field is masked, and building the model anyway is a contract breach you will have to disclose in every operational due diligence you face for the next decade. The narrow surviving case is a vendor who is indifferent and strips the field for engineering or GDPR-hygiene reasons rather than contractual ones. That case exists, but you establish it with two phone calls in week zero, not with a research plan. Note also that asking the vendor for permission on a defined list tells them exactly which institutions you care about.

**2. Nobody counted the tradeable names.** The plan's own "graceful retreat" — neobanks, brokers, BNPL in UK/DE/ES — is where the identification signal actually is, for exactly the reasons the plan gives. Now look at the fintech list in Section 3: Revolut, N26, bunq, Monzo, Starling, Trade Republic, Scalable, Trading 212, Zopa, Younited, Alma, Scalapay, Wise, Klarna, eToro. Check the current status of each yourself, but as of writing the overwhelming majority are private, and the two most prominent that have listed (Klarna, eToro) listed in the US, not Europe. You are proposing to build a European identification engine whose highest-confidence output is a set of companies you cannot trade. Meanwhile the segment that *is* listed and liquid — incumbent universal and mid-cap banks — is where the fingerprints are weakest, the twins problem is worst, and, per point 3 below, the panel physically cannot see the relevant flows.

Do this on paper in week one: enumerate European-listed financials where (a) between-quarter KPI visibility is genuinely poor, (b) the stock moves on that KPI, (c) the retail flow footprint is visible in a bank-transaction panel, and (d) there is no indistinguishable peer. My prior is you land somewhere between ten and twenty-five names. Then price what a mediocre-precision quarterly nowcast on twenty names is worth. If that number doesn't clear the cost of the panel plus a quarter of analyst time plus the compliance overhead, you're done, and you found out for free.

**3. The panel sees incumbents through the wrong end of the telescope, and the plan half-knows this.** Section 7 gets it right: panelists link their primary account, so a bank's own customers' internal flows are invisible. The implication the plan doesn't follow through: for an incumbent retail bank, what the panel observes is *outbound transfers from other people's primary accounts into that bank* — i.e. the bank as a secondary relationship. That population is small, unrepresentative, and its growth has no reliable relationship to reported deposits. So the nowcast test will fail for incumbents by construction, not because the mapping is wrong.

This compounds with a sample-size problem the plan never checks. The marquee feature is the NUTS3 location quotient. There are on the order of 1,300 NUTS3 regions in the EU. To get a stable geographic profile vector you need thousands of transacting panelists per ID. For a mid-cap Italian or Spanish bank in a panel with maybe low-hundreds-of-thousands of panelists in that country, you will have hundreds, not thousands. So the discriminating features require scale, the institutions with scale are the ones the panel sees worst, and the ones the panel sees well are private. That pincer is the project.

---

## Step-level breaks

**§3, label design.** 200–300 labels across six countries and five types is ~10 per cell. Sixty held out. You then propose to stratify holdout accuracy by country, type, size quartile *and* difficulty quintile. The confidence interval on rank-1 accuracy at n=60 is roughly ±12pp; on a size-quartile subset it's ±25pp. Your own kill criterion — "rank-1 below 65% for the top size quartile" — is not measurable at that sample size. Either raise the label count by an order of magnitude or abandon statistical framing entirely for case-by-case forensics.

**§3, label source (i) is the worst possible training set and the "difficulty score" doesn't fix it.** IDs whose strings leak leak for a systematic pipeline reason. A subjective 1–5 difficulty score does not let you reweight to the masked population. Two things would: inverse-propensity weighting, where you model P(labelled | observable ID features available for *all* IDs — size, country, type, morphology) and reweight the holdout; and a synthetic-mask control, where you hash the *named merchant* IDs and see whether the same pipeline recovers them. The second gives you thousands of unbiased labels on the machinery, at the cost that merchants aren't financials.

**§3, label source (ii) is used backwards.** A purchased named feed for one country is the only unbiased, complete, non-self-selected label set you will ever get. The plan reserves it strictly for training and forbids using it for validation in that country. That is exactly inverted. Train on the biased leak-set, *test* on the fully named country. Otherwise you have no honest read on precision anywhere.

**§4/§5, circularity between the matching model and the economic validation.** Stage two includes "Pearson correlation of monthly panel active customers against quarterly reported deposits" as a *pair-scoring feature*. Section 6 then presents nowcast performance as an independent economic test. It isn't independent of the model — only of the labels. If KPI correlation is an input to the match, discovering that matched IDs track KPIs is tautological. Fix: identify on geography, demographics, morphology, co-occurrence and events only; quarantine every reported-KPI relationship as pure validation. This costs match accuracy and it is not optional.

**§6, the nowcast test can pass under a wrong mapping.** European bank deposit growth is dominated by common factors — the rate cycle, national M2, term-deposit migration. Two banks in the same country have highly correlated YoY deposit growth. Mapping ID→Bank A when it is truly Bank B, same country, will still produce respectable pooled R². The permutation test is the right instinct but the design puts it in a vice: permute within loose strata and the test is uninformative; permute within country×type, as written, and the true mapping likely fails because the residual idiosyncratic signal is small. What actually discriminates is firm-specific timing: strip the country×type common factor from both series and test whether panel residuals predict reported residuals, and test whether the panel moves on the right dates for firm-specific events (a deposit promo, a rebrand, an outage, an acquisition close). Also: eight overlapping quarters with 2024–2025 evaluation is six to eight points per name. You cannot ship a per-name identification on a pooled fixed-effects R² — you ship names individually, so the evidence must be per-name.

**§4, event fingerprints — right family, wrong method, no null.** If a step change at the Bankia absorption is "nearly identifying on its own," then build the corporate-event calendar first and hand-search discontinuities. That gets you your first twenty IDs in three weeks with no labels, no logit and no calibration. As specified, PELT with BIC-tuned penalty on 24–48 monthly points will give you changepoints everywhere or nowhere, and ±45-day matching against a calendar of hundreds of events across 700 candidates will generate substantial coincidental matches. You must compute the null explicitly by shuffling the event calendar and reporting the spurious-match rate. Without that number, "matched changepoint count" is not evidence.

**§5, stages two and three are over-built.** Conditional logit assumes IIA, which twins violate directly — near-identical candidates split probability, both fall below 0.90, and your shippable set becomes precisely the names with no close peer. That's conservative and honest, but it means coverage is low and structurally non-random, which you should state up front rather than discover in week eleven. Isotonic calibration on a held-out fold of forty-odd observations will be an overfit step function; use Platt or beta, or drop calibrated-probability language and report empirical precision by margin decile. And cut stage three entirely. Hungarian assignment over 700 candidates buys nothing when you care about twenty names and when the plan already concedes injectivity fails for the co-op networks and multi-brand groups. It adds a failure mode where one bad match cascades.

**§5, the 700-way framing is the wrong construct.** You do not need to rank 700 candidates. You need to answer "is this ID Revolut / Trade Republic / Bank X?" for the names you would trade, with a strong "none of the above" prior and cheerfully low coverage. Reframing as a small set of binary hypothesis tests removes most of the statistical difficulty and all of stage three.

**§8, the timeline is off by a quarter.** Legal clearance *and* data delivery *and* the 700-row candidate table in weeks one to two is not real. European alt-data contracting plus DPIA plus environment onboarding is routinely two to three months. And branch-count-by-NUTS3 for 700 institutions is not a two-week job — OSM `operator` tagging is sparse and inconsistent outside DE/UK/FR.

**§3, unverified data assumptions that could end it on day three.** Is the hash per-counterparty or salted per-panelist? If per-panelist, wallet co-occurrence, ID-level aggregation and the whole approach die instantly. Is the hash stable across the 48-month window, or rotated? Does a clean "financial counterparty ID" field exist at all, or is it a mush of P2P transfers, ATM operators and processors — which is the usual reason this field gets stripped? What is the distinct-ID count and its size distribution, and panelists per country? Get a sample extract and answer these before anything else.

**Minor but fix them:** discarding hand-label disagreements rather than adjudicating deliberately manufactures the easy-label bias you elsewhere worry about — adjudicate, log it, and keep the disagreements as a hard-stratum test set. Kill criteria should be stated in tradeable terms ("≥N European-listed names at 95% precision *with* demonstrated per-name incremental skill over an app-download-plus-consensus baseline"), not "40 institutions," which forty private neobanks would satisfy while the project failed.

**One free-lunch check worth doing in week one:** for neobanks, app MAU and download data may already nowcast the KPI as well as the panel does. If so, the panel adds nothing over data you can buy far more cheaply, in the exact segment where identification is easiest. That's a one-week test on the handful of names with public customer-count disclosure, and it can kill the strongest-looking part of the project before you spend anything.

---

## The cheaper version

Five weeks, four sequential gates, stop at the first failure.

**Week 0 (two days).** Price a named financial-counterparty feed from the vendor and read the licence. Named feed available and affordable → buy it, project over. Explicitly prohibited → escalate to compliance and expect a no. Neither → continue.

**Week 1 (paper only, no data).** Enumerate the tradeable universe: European-listed financials with poor intra-quarter visibility, a panel-visible retail flow footprint, adequate country sample, and no indistinguishable twin. Attach an alpha estimate. Under ~15 names or under your cost hurdle → stop. Run the app-data-versus-panel test on any neobank with public disclosure while you're here.

**Weeks 2–3 (sample extract).** Hash stability and salting, ID count and size distribution, panelists per country, whether the financial-ID field is clean. Also compute, empirically, how many transacting panelists your ten largest target institutions actually have, and whether that supports a NUTS3 geography vector. Any of these fails → stop.

**Weeks 3–5 (forensics on the target list only).** Build the corporate-event calendar for your twenty names — this is the durable asset and the plan is right about that. Hand-match discontinuities: launches, market entries and exits, merger completions, rebrands, licence changes, rate-promo dates. Compute the shuffled-calendar null so you know your false-match rate. If you cannot confidently identify five of twenty names this way, the 200-feature model will not rescue you, because forensics is strictly easier than statistics here.

Only if all four gates pass do you commission the full build — and then with the leak-set bias correction, the KPI features quarantined out of matching, a fully-named country as the test set rather than the training set, per-name residual validation, and stage three deleted.

The honest summary is that this plan is a well-executed answer to a question that should have been dismantled commercially and legally before anyone designed a conditional logit. Find out whether there are fifteen tradeable names and whether you're allowed to do this at all. Both answers are available for the cost of a week.

# Research Plan: Guarantor Removal on a Hyperscaler–Foundry/ASIC SPV as a Second-Source Signal

## 0. First, pin the fact pattern down

Before any analysis, the analyst spends the first day establishing exactly what happened, because the idea as stated contains three unverified assumptions: that a guarantee existed, that it was *removed* rather than *released on a pre-agreed schedule*, and that the hyperscaler's economic commitment changed as a result.

Identify the SPV by legal name and jurisdiction. Work from the disclosure that triggered the idea backward to primary documents: SEC EDGAR full-text search (efts.sec.gov, covers 2001+) on the SPV name plus terms like "Guaranty," "Guarantor Release," "Parent Guarantee," "Capacity Reservation Agreement"; the 8-K Item 1.01/1.02/2.03 stream for both parties; exhibit lists (EX-10.x) for amendments and amended-and-restated credit agreements; the 10-K/20-F footnotes on Guarantees and Indemnifications (ASC 460), Variable Interest Entities (ASC 810), Contractual Obligations, and Related Party Transactions. For non-US counterparties: Taiwan's MOPS, where listed companies must disclose endorsement/guarantee (背書保證) balances monthly and material contract changes promptly; Korea's DART; Japan's EDINET; Luxembourg RCS/RESA and Irish CRO, where guarantee deeds for financing SPVs are frequently filed in full. Pull LSEG LPC DealScan for the loan tranche history including the guarantor list at each amendment, and Bloomberg CACS/DDIS for the SPV's debt if it issues. Rating agency pre-sale and issuer reports (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) are the single richest source: if a guarantee disappears, the agency explains in prose what replaced it and whether notching changed. Also run UCC-1 and UCC-3 searches in the relevant Secretary of State databases — a terminated financing statement or a change in secured party tells you whether collateral moved with the guarantee.

The deliverable from this step is a one-page fact sheet: entity chart, capital structure of the SPV, who guaranteed what before, what the amendment changed, effective date, and — critically — the disclosure date versus the effective date.

## 1. The hypothesis, stated so it can be wrong

**H1 (the researcher's thesis):** The hyperscaler has qualified or is qualifying an alternate supplier, and is deliberately reducing its financial exposure to the primary provider's capacity build, shifting utilization and capex risk onto the supplier's balance sheet. Prediction: the supplier's share of that program declines, contract liabilities and prepayments stagnate or fall, and evidence of a second design win appears within 12–18 months.

**H0 (the boring explanation, and the base case):** The guarantee release was pre-negotiated at inception, triggered automatically by a completion test, DSCR test, or ratings/leverage condition, or was removed for accounting reasons — to avoid a guarantee liability under ASC 460, to avoid consolidating the SPV as a VIE under ASC 810, or to keep the obligation out of the contractual obligations table. Economic commitment unchanged.

**H2 (risk transformation, not risk reduction):** The guarantee was replaced by an economically equivalent or stronger instrument — a take-or-pay capacity reservation with liquidated damages, a prepayment, a keepwell, or an equity contribution agreement. This is the most likely way the researcher's thesis is *directionally wrong in a costly way*, because it looks like disengagement and is actually deeper commitment.

**H3 (financing maturation):** The SPV became standalone-financeable — construction complete, third-party customers added, subsidy tranche received (CHIPS Act, METI, EU Chips Act conditions often constrain ownership and support structures) — and lenders no longer required the credit enhancement.

**H4 (program de-scoping):** Not second sourcing, but shrinkage or cancellation of the program. Worse for the supplier than H1 and requires a different trade.

**H5 (regulatory/tax):** Export control, antitrust, transfer pricing, or subsidy-eligibility restructuring.

The research question is not "is H1 true" but "what is the posterior probability of each, and which is mispriced."

## 2. Document forensics: the decisive work

Redline the pre- and post-amendment agreements clause by clause and populate a structured extraction table with these fields: minimum volume or take-or-pay commitment (units and dollars), term, liquidated damages on shortfall, termination-for-convenience fee schedule, prepayment/deposit balance and refundability, capacity reservation fee, exclusivity and its carve-outs, explicit alternate-source or second-source permissions, IP ownership and license scope (does the hyperscaler own the RTL, or license the SerDes/HBM PHY/chiplet interconnect from the supplier?), step-in rights, change-of-control, most-favored-nation pricing, and any keepwell, equity contribution, or comfort letter that appears where the guarantee used to be.

Then check the *original* agreement for a defined "Guarantee Release Date," "Completion Date," "Sponsor Support Termination," or similar. If the release was automatic on a milestone, H0 wins and the idea is largely dead as a signal — though it may still be tradeable if the market misreads it, which is a separate and useful finding.

Use Covenant Review, Xtract Research, or 9fin if the SPV debt is rated and syndicated; they publish clause-level analyses that will save days.

## 3. Did economic commitment actually change? Follow the money

Independent of the legal documents, test whether the hyperscaler's cash and obligations to this supplier grew or shrank. On the supplier side, track quarter by quarter for eight quarters before and however many after: contract liabilities and deferred revenue, "advances from customers" or customer deposits, accounts receivable concentration, the 10% customer disclosure (ASC 280) or equivalent, inventory and days of inventory, purchase commitments to *its* suppliers (a supplier that has quietly lost a customer stops committing to CoWoS/HBM/substrate), and capex versus depreciation. On the hyperscaler side, the contractual obligations table, "other commitments" footnote, and any disclosed prepayments.

The critical test for H2: if prepayments or contract liabilities rose in the same period the guarantee fell away, the hyperscaler substituted cash for credit support and the thesis inverts. If both the guarantee and the prepayments fell, H1 or H4 is live.

## 4. Independent evidence on the second source

Do not let the SPV document carry the whole argument. Assemble corroboration from four independent channels, each with a specific source:

**Design and tape-out evidence.** Monthly revenue disclosures from Taiwanese design-service and ASIC houses (Alchip, GUC, Faraday) and from TSMC/UMC — Taiwan's monthly revenue reporting regime gives you a high-frequency series most models ignore. Watch for NRE-driven step-ups at a candidate second source. Cross-check with Hot Chips, ISSCC, and OCP Global Summit presentations, where hyperscalers disclose accelerator and NIC architecture details and frequently name partners. Check USPTO assignment records and co-assignment patterns; a switch in ASIC partner shows up in co-invented patents 18–24 months ahead of revenue.

**Supply chain flow.** OSAT and test house monthly revenues (Amkor, ASE/SPIL, KYEC), substrate makers (Ibiden, Shinko, AT&S), and ODM assemblers (Quanta, Wiwynn, Celestica, Jabil, Foxconn Industrial Internet). Panjiva/S&P Global bills of lading and Taiwan/Korea customs aggregates at the HS-code level — noting that hyperscaler ASIC flows usually route through ODMs, so entity-level attribution is weak; use these as corroboration, never as primary evidence.

**Labor and organizational signal.** Revelio Labs or LinkUp job-posting data on the hyperscaler's silicon organization and on candidate second suppliers: postings referencing a specific EDA flow, packaging technology, or "dual-source qualification" are informative. Track senior IC engineering moves between the hyperscaler and the candidate alternate.

**Management language.** Run a systematic language diff across the supplier's last eight earnings calls and the hyperscaler's, using AlphaSense or Bloomberg transcript search: frequency and framing of "customer concentration," "second source," "multi-vendor," "prototype," "ramp," "qualification," and the supplier's habit of numbering customers. Note hedging changes, not just topic changes.

Existing Tegus/AlphaSense expert transcripts should be mined before commissioning new expert calls; if new calls are needed, route through compliance with scripted questions that avoid the SPV's contractual terms (see pitfalls).

## 5. Base rates from analogous restructurings

Build a hand-curated case book of 20–35 events in capital-intensive supply chains where a large customer's credit support for a supplier-affiliated SPV or JV was removed, reduced, or restructured. Seed list: the WD/Kioxia Flash Ventures guarantee and lease structures; Micron–Inotera; Apple–GT Advanced (the cautionary case on prepayment-plus-security structures); Apple–Amkor Arizona; TSMC JASM's equity partners; Intel's Brookfield and Apollo semiconductor co-investment programs; Bosch–GlobalFoundries Dresden; and, as adjacent analogs, telecom fiber and data center JV structures (Meta–KKR, Microsoft–BlackRock AIP, Oracle-linked vehicles).

For each case, record the stated reason, whether an offsetting commitment appeared, and the outcome at +8 quarters: did the customer's revenue share at that supplier decline more than 15 percentage points? Did consensus revenue estimates for the supplier fall? This sample is far too small for regression; treat it as structured case-based reasoning with a scoring rubric, and report the base rate honestly as, say, "4 of 22 cases were followed by material share loss" rather than dressing it up as a probability model.

## 6. Market tests: is this priced?

Run a standard event study on the supplier's equity around both the effective date and the disclosure date. Estimator: a four-factor market model (Fama-French three factors plus momentum) augmented with an orthogonalized SOX index return, estimated over 250 trading days ending 30 days before the event, with CARs measured over (-1,+1), (0,+5), and (0,+20). For the base-rate sample, use the Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen standardized cross-sectional test, with the Corrado rank test as a non-parametric robustness check given small n and fat tails.

Extend to credit: the supplier's CDS spread change versus CDX IG, and bond OAS from TRACE. And to options: 30- and 90-day implied vol and 25-delta skew around the date.

The key read is not the sign of the CAR but its *magnitude relative to nothing*. If the disclosure was buried in an exhibit and CAR is statistically indistinguishable from zero on normal volume, the information is likely unpriced — which is the entire investment case. If there was a clear negative move on elevated volume, the idea is already consensus and the remaining question is whether it overshot.

## 7. Sizing the economics and expressing the view

Build a program-level model for the supplier: units, ASP, gross margin, NRE versus production revenue, and the capex the SPV was built to support. Three scenarios at a two-year horizon: (a) dual-source with a 70/30 volume split, (b) financing optimization with no share change, (c) program de-scoping with 40%+ volume decline. Translate each to revenue, EPS, and a defensible multiple, and weight by the posterior probabilities from Sections 2–5.

Note the asymmetry of expression: this is almost never a trade in the hyperscaler, where the program is immaterial to consolidated earnings. The trade lives in the primary supplier (short or underweight), the candidate second source (long), and the second-order names whose economics are share-agnostic (OSAT, substrate, design services), which can serve as a hedge or as the cleanest long if you believe the program grows regardless of who wins it. A pair — short primary versus long alternate, beta- and SOX-neutralized — isolates the share-shift view from AI-capex direction, which is the dominant risk factor and one you are not trying to take.

## 8. Kill criteria, stated in advance

The thesis is dead if any of the following is found: the original agreement contains a scheduled or milestone-triggered guarantee release; the amendment leaves minimum volume commitments unchanged or increases them; contract liabilities or customer prepayments at the supplier rise in the two quarters around the event; a rating agency attributes the release to construction completion, third-party customer diversification, or subsidy conditions; or no tape-out, NRE, or hiring evidence of a second source appears within twelve months of the guarantee change. Write these down before the work starts and hold to them.

## 9. Pitfalls to watch

The dominant error is conflating a legal guarantee with an economic commitment. Sophisticated buyers routinely trade a guarantee for a take-or-pay, which increases their exposure while shrinking the disclosed one. A related error is entity confusion: "removed as guarantor" often means removed and *replaced* by another group entity — sometimes a stronger one — and SPV naming conventions make this easy to misread. Read the entity chart, not the headline.

Custom silicon is not fungible. Even where a second source is genuinely qualified, switching depends on who owns the RTL and whether the SerDes, HBM PHY, and chiplet interconnect IP travel with the design; packaging and system qualification alone run 12–24 months. A correct thesis can lose money for two years, so the timeline must be built into position sizing and into the choice between equity, options, and credit.

Beware confirmation bias in the corroborating channels — Taiwan supply chain press in particular reports directional rumors that are frequently right in substance and wrong in magnitude and timing. Require two independent channels before upgrading a hypothesis.

On compliance: contractual terms of a private SPV agreement are exactly the kind of information an expert network call can turn into MNPI. Keep expert calls to industry structure, qualification timelines, and general practice; never to the specific contract. Document the provenance of every input, confirm licensing terms on customs data, and have compliance pre-clear the source list.

Finally, guard against the small-sample seduction of the base-rate case book. Twenty hand-picked cases with survivorship in what got disclosed will not generate a reliable probability. Use it to structure judgment, not to manufacture precision.

## 10. Timeline and deliverables

Days 1–3: fact sheet and entity chart, all primary documents pulled. Days 4–7: clause-level redline and extraction table, financial commitment reconciliation, rating agency review. Days 8–11: second-source corroboration across the four channels, base-rate case book. Days 12–13: event study and pricing tests, scenario model. Day 14: a decision memo containing the hypothesis scorecard with explicit posteriors and the evidence weighting behind each, the recommended expression with sizing and hedge, the kill criteria, and a monitoring dashboard — Taiwanese monthly revenue prints, EDGAR/MOPS/DART filing alerts on the named entities, rating actions, and OSAT revenue — with named owners and a weekly refresh.

## Verdict

The analytical instincts here are good — the hypothesis set is well-built, H2 is the sharpest thing in the document, and pre-committing kill criteria is right. But the plan is structured to prove the thesis carefully rather than to kill the project cheaply, and the sequencing guarantees you spend a week on work that has a high probability of being impossible before you ever run the two tests that decide whether the project is worth doing. It is also over-scoped by roughly 3x against its own timeline.

More fundamentally: I don't think this is a two-week project. It's a half-day screen that, maybe one time in ten, becomes a two-week project.

## The structural break: "new SPV" is incompatible with Section 2

The idea says the hyperscaler was removed as guarantor **on a new SPV**. Section 2 — described as "the decisive work" — is a clause-by-clause redline of pre- and post-amendment agreements and a search of the *original* agreement for a defined Guarantee Release Date.

On a new SPV there is no pre-amendment agreement. If the guarantee "disappeared" during formation or syndication, what you are looking at is a term that changed between a marketing term sheet, a commitment letter, and executed docs — a negotiation artifact, driven by lender appetite, rating agency treatment, and parent-level debt capacity, not by silicon roadmaps. The spine of the plan is designed for a mid-life amendment and the fact pattern describes something else.

Before anything: establish whether an *executed* guarantee ever existed, or whether the analyst is comparing a draft/preliminary structure to a final one. That is a 30-minute question and it kills or reframes the entire project.

## Document availability is an unexamined gate

Section 2's extraction table wants minimum volume commitments, liquidated damages on shortfall, termination-for-convenience schedules, MFN pricing, step-in rights, and IP license scope. For a hyperscaler–foundry SPV, that document will almost certainly not be publicly available:

- Nothing about a single SPV is material to a $2–3T registrant, so no 8-K Item 1.01 and no EX-10.
- Where an exhibit *is* filed, exactly those terms are redacted under Reg S-K 601(b)(10)(iv) as competitively harmful.
- Taiwan MOPS discloses endorsement/guarantee *balances*, not clauses. DART and EDINET are the same.
- Lux RCS and Irish CRO filings are real but only for those jurisdictions, and typically the security package, not the offtake.

The plan should have an explicit gate at Day 1: *do the documents exist in unredacted form?* If not, Sections 2 and most of 7 collapse and the entire exercise becomes inference from indirect evidence — a much weaker and much cheaper piece of work. Budgeting four days to redlining documents you probably can't obtain is the single largest scheduling error.

## The two cheapest decisive tests are missing or buried

**Materiality screen on the supplier.** The plan correctly notes the trade is never in the hyperscaler because the program is immaterial to consolidated earnings — then never applies the same test to the supplier. If the primary provider is TSMC or Samsung, one hyperscaler ASIC program is low-single-digit revenue and the stock trades on aggregate AI capex, N2 pricing, and HPC mix. A 30-point share shift is unexpressible. The thesis is only tradeable if the supplier is a concentrated ASIC vendor (Broadcom, Marvell, Alchip, GUC, Socionext). This is an hour of work and belongs at hour one, not implicitly at Section 7.

**Is the conclusion already consensus?** Section 6 tests whether the *guarantee event* is priced. That is the wrong test. The relevant question is whether the *second-sourcing conclusion* is priced. Vendor splits on hyperscaler accelerator programs are among the most heavily covered questions in the sector — discussed on every sell-side call and in Taiwan supply chain notes weekly. An unpriced signal that supports an already-consensus conclusion is worth nothing. Four hours of reading transcripts and recent notes tells you whether there's anything left to discover.

**The rating agency report.** This is listed inside a long Day 1–3 source dump. It is probably the single highest-yield document in the whole plan — if the SPV is rated, the agency explains in prose what the guarantee was replaced by and whether notching changed, which resolves H0/H2/H3 directly. Pull it first, alone, before anything else.

## Logic and mechanism problems

**Missing hypothesis (H6, bullish).** The guarantee may have come off because the program *grew* past the point where the parent wanted the obligation on its balance sheet or in its contractual obligations table. Bigger commitment, less disclosure. This is the mirror image of H1, it is at least as likely, and it is absent from the hypothesis set.

**The ASC 810 reasoning in H0 is loose.** Dropping a parent guarantee does not by itself avoid VIE consolidation — the analysis turns on power over significant activities plus variable interests, and a take-or-pay capacity reservation is itself a variable interest that can force consolidation. That means "removed for accounting reasons" and H2 "replaced by an economically equivalent take-or-pay" are partly mutually exclusive. Conversely, if the hyperscaler's filings show it does not consolidate the SPV, that meaningfully constrains how much economic commitment can be hiding elsewhere. That is a cheap, decisive test buried in a footnote reference.

**The causal mechanism is never argued.** Guarantee structures are set by treasury and capital markets people negotiating with lenders and rating agencies, frequently with no line of sight into the product org's sourcing roadmap. The plan assumes this decision encodes sourcing intent. Absent a stated mechanism, the honest prior on H1 as the unique explanation is 5–10%, not the 30–40% the resource allocation implies.

## Methodology that won't hold up

- **Event study, n=1.** Single-name CAR(-1,+1) against 3%/day idiosyncratic vol tells you nothing, and for a disclosure buried in an exhibit there is no clean event date — the market learns gradually, so the design is misspecified. BMP and Corrado are cross-sectional tests; you don't have a cross-section.
- **The case book is a collage, not a base rate.** Apple/GT Advanced (prepayment-with-security to a distressed micro-cap), Meta/KKR (data center JV financing), Bosch/GF Dresden (EU subsidy), WD/Kioxia (lease structures) are not the same phenomenon. Reporting "4 of 22" invites false precision even with the disclaimer. Cut to the 3–5 genuinely analogous cases and read them qualitatively.
- **Patent co-assignment.** Hyperscaler ASIC work is typically work-for-hire with the hyperscaler owning; co-assignment often doesn't exist. The asserted 18–24 month lead is unsupported. Low expected yield.
- **CDS/OAS on the supplier.** If the supplier is large, credit is insensitive to one program; if it's Alchip or GUC, there's no CDS. Dead either way.
- **Customs/Panjiva.** The plan correctly says it can never be primary evidence, then still budgets licensing and days for it. Drop it.
- **Job postings.** Very noisy; hyperscalers post generically. Optional at best.

## Compliance is aimed at the wrong entity

The plan protects against expert calls on the SPV's contract terms. Correct, but the larger exposure is on the *second source*: an unannounced design win at a small-cap ASIC house is extremely material there, and a single confirming call converts a legal mosaic into MNPI on that name. Also unexamined: the provenance of the original observation. How did the analyst learn a guarantor was removed on a private SPV? That should be documented and cleared before any work starts.

## The trade

Short primary / long alternate, SOX- and beta-neutral, is not the clean isolation it appears to be. If the alternate is a Taiwan-listed design house, the pair is dominated by liquidity, borrow, and retail flow, and the short leg carries almost no signal because the program is immaterial to the primary. What you actually have is a small long in the alternate with a factor hedge attached. Size it that way or don't do it. Also check Taiwan short-sale and foreign-investor mechanics before assuming the hedge is executable.

## The cheaper version

Half a day, in this order:

1. Provenance of the observation, and did an executed guarantee ever exist. (30 min)
2. Pull the rating agency report on the SPV. It likely states the reason outright. (30 min)
3. Materiality: what share of the supplier's revenue/EPS is this program? If under ~5%, stop. (1 hr)
4. Is second-sourcing on this program already consensus? Transcripts, recent notes, Taiwan press. If yes, stop. (2 hrs)
5. Does the hyperscaler consolidate the SPV, and did that change? (30 min)

If all five clear — executed guarantee genuinely removed, RA doesn't explain it away, supplier is concentrated enough to trade, second-source is not consensus — then commission the two-week version, with the document-availability gate at the top and the case book and event study cut. My expectation is that step 2 or step 4 kills it.

## What to keep

The H0–H5 framing, the guarantee-versus-economic-commitment distinction, the pre-committed kill criteria, the note that a correct thesis can lose money for two years on qualification timelines, and the Taiwan monthly revenue monitoring at the design-service houses — that last one is genuinely the highest-yield, lowest-cost channel in the document and should be running continuously regardless of what happens to this idea.

# Research Plan: Does Earnings-Call Sentiment Predict Peer-Relative Outperformance?

## 1. The hypothesis, stated tightly

The loose version of the idea — "positive tone on calls means the stock goes up" — is almost certainly true and almost certainly useless, because tone is mechanically correlated with the earnings surprise the call is discussing. The tradable version is narrower:

**H1 (information content).** After controlling for the reported earnings surprise, guidance revisions, and the stock's contemporaneous price reaction, the tone of management's *unscripted* answers in the Q&A section contains incremental information about the firm's competitive position, and this information is impounded slowly.

**H2 (peer-relative).** Because tone is contaminated by industry-wide conditions (every semiconductor CEO sounds gloomy in a downturn), the signal is cleanest when both the sentiment measure and the return are measured relative to a peer group. Cross-sectionally demeaning tone within a sector-quarter should *increase* predictive power, not decrease it.

**H3 (mechanism).** If the signal is real, residual tone should predict future *fundamentals* — the next quarter's earnings surprise and the intervening analyst estimate revisions — not just returns. This is the test that separates a genuine information signal from a data-mined return pattern.

The primary economic question we are answering: is there a sector-neutral long/short signal here with a post-cost information ratio above ~0.5 on a monthly-rebalanced, three-month-holding basis, in the top 1,500 US stocks by market cap?

## 2. Data

**Transcripts.** S&P Global Market Intelligence (Capital IQ) transcripts, 2006–2024, accessed via the Xpressfeed transcript tables. Capital IQ is preferred over Refinitiv StreetEvents because it tags speaker role (executive vs. analyst), section (presentation vs. Q&A), and component type at the paragraph level, which we need for H1. Critically, we take the **call start and end timestamps**, not the transcript publication timestamp, and we verify against a sample of 200 calls that the transcript's "most recent version" flag is being handled correctly — Capital IQ revises transcripts, and naive pulls give you the corrected version with a stale date.

**Returns and prices.** CRSP daily, US common shares (share codes 10, 11), primary listing, plus CRSP delisting returns.

**Fundamentals and estimates.** Compustat quarterly (point-in-time via the Compustat Snapshot / unrestated file where available; otherwise lag reported items by the actual filing date from the SEC full-text index). I/B/E/S Detail History for consensus EPS, actuals, and analyst-level revisions — using the *unadjusted* files to avoid the well-known split-adjustment rounding problem in the summary file.

**Peer groups.** Primary definition: GICS sub-industry (level 4), requiring at least 5 firms in the group in that quarter. Robustness definition: Hoberg-Phillips TNIC-3 industries (text-based, time-varying), which better capture product-market competitors and are updated annually. A third check: analyst co-coverage peers from I/B/E/S (firms sharing ≥3 covering analysts).

**Universe.** Stocks in the top 1,500 by market cap at each month-end, price ≥ $5, with a transcript in the prior 63 trading days. Expect roughly 1,200–1,400 names per month with usable calls after 2010; coverage is thinner and biased toward large caps before 2008, which is why the sample starts in 2006 and the in-sample period starts in 2008.

## 3. Constructing the sentiment measures

Build three families so that no result depends on one vendor's black box.

**(a) Dictionary tone.** Loughran-McDonald 2023 master dictionary. Net tone = (positive − negative) / (positive + negative + 1), computed separately for: full call, prepared remarks, management's Q&A answers, and analysts' questions. Also compute the LM *uncertainty* and *litigious* word rates, and a hedging count using a hand-built list ("we believe," "should," "roughly," "somewhat," "we'll see," "hard to say").

**(b) Transformer sentiment.** FinBERT (ProsusAI variant, pretrained on Reuters TRC2 1996–2007 and fine-tuned on Financial PhraseBank) scored at the sentence level, then aggregated as the mean of (P(positive) − P(negative)). FinBERT's known training cutoff matters: it lets us score the whole 2008–2024 sample without look-ahead contamination. **Do not** use GPT-4-class models for the primary signal — their training corpora extend through the test period and they may have memorized outcomes. If we want an LLM comparison, run it only on the 2023–2024 holdout as a descriptive check, and disclose it as contaminated.

**(c) Within-firm tone change.** ΔTone = current call tone minus the firm's trailing four-call mean. This differences out the CEO's baseline verbosity and the firm's boilerplate, which is the single largest source of cross-sectional variation in raw tone.

**Orthogonalization.** For each call, regress each tone measure cross-sectionally (within sector-quarter) on: standardized unexpected earnings (SUE, defined as actual minus median I/B/E/S consensus in the 90 days before the call, scaled by the standard deviation of analyst estimates), revenue surprise, the change in management guidance midpoint versus prior guidance, the stock's [−1, +1] abnormal return around the call, log market cap, book-to-market, 12-1 momentum, and the prior quarter's tone. **The residual from this regression is the signal.** Save the raw measures too, so we can show how much of the apparent predictive power is just the surprise in disguise.

Finally, standardize the residual within sector-quarter to a z-score, winsorized at ±3. This is `TONE_RESID`.

## 4. Dependent variables

Peer-relative return is defined as the stock's return minus the equal-weighted return of its GICS sub-industry peers (excluding itself), over:
- **[0, +1]**: the announcement window — a test of whether tone is *news* at all.
- **[+2, +63]**: the drift window — the tradable question, starting two days after the call so we are not assuming instantaneous execution.
- **[+2, +126]**: persistence.
- **Placebo: [−63, −2]**: sentiment should *not* predict past peer-relative returns beyond what momentum controls absorb. If it does, we have a leakage or timing bug.

For fundamental tests: next quarter's SUE, and the cumulative change in the FY1 consensus estimate over [+2, +63], scaled by price.

## 5. Estimation

**Step 1 — Panel regressions.** Regress each dependent variable on `TONE_RESID` with sector × quarter fixed effects and standard errors double-clustered by firm and calendar quarter. Report the coefficient in basis points per one-standard-deviation of tone. This is the cleanest statement of the effect size.

**Step 2 — Fama-MacBeth.** Every month-end, take all stocks with a call in the prior 63 trading days, run a cross-sectional regression of the next month's peer-relative return on `TONE_RESID` plus size, book-to-market, momentum, short-term reversal, gross profitability, asset growth, and SUE. Average the 200-odd monthly coefficients, Newey-West with 6 lags. This is the specification most comparable to the published literature and the one a portfolio manager will recognize.

**Step 3 — Portfolios.** Each month-end, sort within sector into quintiles on `TONE_RESID`. Long the top quintile, short the bottom, sector-neutral by construction, holding three months in overlapping tranches (one-third of the book rebalances monthly, Jegadeesh-Titman style). Run both equal-weighted and a capacity-realistic weighting (weight ∝ 20-day median dollar volume, capped at 2% per name). Evaluate the return series against the Fama-French five factors plus momentum plus short-term reversal, and — importantly — against a post-earnings-announcement-drift factor built from SUE-sorted portfolios, since PEAD is the most likely thing this signal is secretly picking up.

**Step 4 — Costs.** Apply a per-side cost of half the Corwin-Schultz effective spread estimate plus 5bp of market impact, and report turnover. The signal turns over roughly once per quarter by construction, so annual two-way turnover should be around 400–600%; at ~15bp round-trip for large caps this is 60–90bp per year of drag, which the gross alpha must clear comfortably.

## 6. Validation

**Sample split.** Estimate and specify everything on 2008–2018. Freeze the specification in writing — signal definition, universe, weighting, holding period — then run 2019–2024 once. Any degradation beyond a 40% haircut in the information ratio is a red flag for overfitting or crowding.

**Cross-market replication.** Rerun the frozen specification on STOXX Europe 600 constituents, 2010–2024 (Capital IQ transcript coverage in Europe is adequate from about 2010, English-language calls only). A signal that works in the US and not in Europe isn't necessarily dead, but it needs an explanation.

**Robustness grid.** Vary: peer definition (GICS sub-industry vs. TNIC-3 vs. co-coverage), sentiment engine (LM vs. FinBERT vs. ΔTone), section (Q&A-only vs. full call), size bucket (top 500 / 501–1500), and holding period (1, 3, 6 months). Report the *full* grid, not the best cell. A real effect should be positive in the large majority of the ~50 cells with the Q&A-only, TNIC-based, ΔTone version strongest; a fragile effect will be positive in a handful.

**Multiple-testing discipline.** With this many specifications, use a t-statistic hurdle of 3.0 for the headline claim, per Harvey-Liu-Zhu, and report the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values across the robustness grid.

**Mechanism test.** H3 above. If `TONE_RESID` predicts next-quarter SUE and analyst revisions with the same sign as returns, we have a story. If it predicts returns but not fundamentals, we should suspect that we're capturing a risk premium or a sentiment-driven mispricing that could reverse — check for reversal in [+127, +252].

**Bug hunts.** Randomize the transcript-to-firm mapping 500 times and confirm the alpha distribution is centered on zero. Shift all call dates forward by exactly one quarter and confirm the signal dies. Both are cheap and catch the most common catastrophic errors.

## 7. Pitfalls to watch

**Timing.** The most likely fatal error. Most calls happen after the close on the announcement day, but a meaningful minority happen the morning of the next trading day, and some happen mid-session. Rule: a call is only actionable from the open of the first trading session that begins at least 30 minutes after the call's *end* timestamp. Verify by hand-checking 100 calls against news archives.

**Tone is not orthogonal to the surprise.** Raw tone and SUE correlate around 0.3–0.4. Check VIFs after orthogonalization; if the residual signal has an R² above ~0.5 against the control set, the residual is mostly noise and the effect size will be unstable.

**Boilerplate and manager fixed effects.** Some CEOs are structurally cheerful. Raw cross-sectional tone sorts will systematically select the same firms every quarter, producing a signal that is really a slow-moving quality or industry tilt. The ΔTone variant and within-firm demeaning are the defense; always report the average within-firm standard deviation of the signal to confirm it actually varies over time.

**Sector composition.** Software companies use more superlatives than utilities. Within-sector standardization handles the mean, but not the variance — check that the signal's standard deviation is comparable across sectors and rescale if not.

**Regime breaks.** COVID (2020Q1–Q2) produced an enormous uniform negative tone shock and a suspension of guidance at hundreds of firms. Report results with and without 2020 excluded. Similarly, the shift to fully scripted calls with pre-submitted questions at some firms post-2021 mechanically reduces Q&A informativeness.

**Crowding.** This literature is public (Mayew-Venkatachalam 2012, Druz et al., a decade of quant vendor products). Expect the effect to be materially weaker post-2015. If the 2019–2024 holdout shows near-zero alpha, that is a finding, not a failure — and it points toward the residual opportunity being in the harder-to-process parts of the call (voice, hesitation, deflection of specific questions) rather than lexical tone.

**Survivorship and selection.** Firms that stop hosting calls are disproportionately distressed. Include them until delisting with CRSP delisting returns, and confirm the signal isn't driven by the tail of firms whose last call was gloomy.

## 8. Deliverables and timeline

Weeks 1–2: data assembly, timestamp validation, universe construction. Week 3: sentiment measure construction and orthogonalization. Weeks 4–5: in-sample panel, Fama-MacBeth, and portfolio results on 2008–2018. Week 6: robustness grid and mechanism tests; freeze specification. Week 7: holdout run and European replication. Week 8: write-up.

The output is a 15-page memo with a single headline table (effect size in bp per SD, in-sample and out-of-sample, gross and net of costs), the full robustness grid as an appendix, and an explicit recommendation on whether the signal warrants a paper-trading allocation.
critique:
## Verdict

This is a well-informed plan — the timestamp discipline, the FinBERT-vs-GPT contamination point, the frozen holdout, the randomization bug hunts, and the explicit "tone is mechanically correlated with SUE" framing are all things most analysts get wrong. I'm not going to manufacture objections about those.

But the plan has one structural problem that makes it likely to produce a confident non-answer, and four specification errors that could produce a confident *wrong* answer. And the sequencing is backwards relative to the decision it's supposed to inform.

---

## 1. The decision rule is arithmetically impossible. This is the biggest flaw.

The stated bar is post-cost IR > 0.5. The stated hurdle is t > 3.0 (Harvey-Liu-Zhu). The holdout is 6 years.

An IR of 0.5 over 6 years produces t ≈ 1.2. Over the 11-year in-sample, t ≈ 1.66. Over the full 17 years, t ≈ 2.1. **You have pre-committed to a hurdle that your own target effect size cannot clear on any subsample, or on the whole thing.** So either the go/no-go is undefined, or you've guaranteed a "no" before writing a line of code.

Same problem with the "40% haircut is a red flag" rule. The standard error on a 6-year out-of-sample IR estimate is roughly 1/√6 ≈ 0.41. A signal with true IR 0.5 will produce measured out-of-sample IRs between roughly 0.0 and 1.0 about two-thirds of the time. A 40% haircut is dead centre of the noise distribution. The rule cannot distinguish decay from sampling error.

**Fix:** do the power calculation in week 0, before anything else, and set the decision rule from it. Realistically that means: (a) pick *one* pre-registered headline specification and accept a t≈2 full-sample hurdle for it, (b) treat the robustness grid as a shrinkage exercise rather than a set of hypothesis tests — report the posterior mean IR after shrinking for the number of specifications tried and make the allocation call on the shrunk number, and (c) replace "40% haircut" with "out-of-sample IR point estimate and its confidence interval; proceed if the lower bound clears zero *and* the point estimate clears costs." If none of that produces a decidable question, the honest conclusion is that this project cannot answer the question with 17 years of data, which is itself worth knowing in week 0 rather than week 8.

## 2. Orthogonalizing tone on the [−1,+1] call-window return does two bad things at once.

First, conceptually: if tone is news, the announcement return *is partly the market's reaction to the tone*. Residualizing on it strips out exactly the informative component and leaves you testing a different, much weaker hypothesis — "tone the market ignored." That may be the underreaction story you want, but it is not H1 as written, and you should not discover the difference in week 5.

Second, mechanically: it induces a spurious positive result. Write R₁ = signal + microstructure noise. Residual tone = tone − b·R₁ carries −b·(noise). Bid-ask bounce and short-horizon reversal make that same noise negatively correlated with the [+2,+63] return. Product of two negatives: **your residualization manufactures positive predictive power out of nothing.** With b > 0 (which it will be, tone and call-window return are strongly positively correlated) this is a live path to a false positive that survives all your bug hunts, because the randomization and date-shift tests both destroy the correlation structure that creates it.

**Fix:** drop the call-window return from the primary orthogonalization. Report "tone | fundamentals" as the primary and "tone | fundamentals + price reaction" as a clearly-labelled secondary underreaction test. If you keep the second, use open-to-close on day 0 only, and add a control for the [+2,+5] return to absorb the bounce reversal.

## 3. "Within sector-quarter" is doing two incompatible jobs, and one of them is degenerate.

You define peers as GICS sub-industry (level 4, ~160 buckets), then say you orthogonalize and standardize "within sector-quarter" and form "quintiles within sector." With 1,500 names, sub-industry cells average ~9 firms. You cannot run a 10-regressor cross-sectional regression in a 9-observation cell. You cannot form quintiles in one either. And z-scoring in a 9-name cell then winsorizing at ±3 is theatre.

Meanwhile the "≥5 firms" peer-group minimum means some dependent variables are a stock's return minus a four-stock equal-weighted average — enormous idiosyncratic noise added to the left-hand side, which directly costs you the statistical power you don't have to spare (see #1).

**Fix:** be explicit and separate the three uses. Orthogonalize pooled with sector×quarter fixed effects (not cell-by-cell regressions). Form quintiles at GICS sector or industry-group level (11 or 25 buckets). Measure the dependent variable as a risk-model residual return or a beta-adjusted sub-industry-relative return with a minimum of 8–10 peers, not a raw difference against four names. Use normalized ranks rather than z-scores throughout.

## 4. Portfolio construction doesn't match the event structure, and the seasonality will bite.

The regressions measure [+2,+63] from the call. The portfolios rebalance monthly on "any call in the prior 63 days," so the average holding carries a signal ~30 trading days stale — you are systematically capturing the back half of the drift and paying full turnover for it. Worse, earnings are clustered in four five-week windows. In the off-season months your "fresh signal" cross-section collapses to off-cycle fiscal-year filers, which are heavily industry-clustered (retail, Nov/Jan-year-end tech). Sector-neutral quintiles in early March will have grotesque sector coverage.

**Fix:** run event-time portfolios as the primary construction — each name enters at the actionable open and is held exactly 63 trading days, weights renormalized daily. That's both the honest test and the implementable version. Then report the P&L decomposed by days-since-call. If the alpha lives in [+2,+10], monthly rebalancing throws most of it away and your entire cost analysis is answering the wrong question.

## 5. Nothing in the design tests the hypothesis you actually stated.

H1 claims the signal carries information about "the firm's competitive position." Your mechanism test is next-quarter SUE and FY1 revisions. Neither is a competitive-position variable, and next-quarter SUE is close to mechanically unpredictable from this call's tone: an upbeat CEO guides up, analysts move to the guide, and SUE resets to zero. You've chosen the one fundamental variable that management's own tone is designed to neutralise.

**Fix:** test what you claimed. Peer-relative revenue growth, peer-relative gross margin change, and peer-relative revision breadth over the next 2–4 quarters. Use FY2 rather than FY1 consensus (less anchored to the current guide). Add the sign of the *next* call's [0,+1] return. And run these peer-relative, to match the return test.

Related: your factor attribution includes a PEAD factor but no **analyst revisions** factor. If H3 works, the most likely reading of the whole exercise is that you've built an expensive proxy for earnings-revision momentum. That has to be in the regression or the memo is not credible.

## 6. FinBERT is the weakest of your three engines, not a neutral third leg.

ProsusAI FinBERT is fine-tuned on Financial PhraseBank — ~4,800 short analyst-style *news* sentences labelled by finance students. Applied sentence-wise to Q&A, it will score factual statements ("revenue grew 12%") as positive, i.e. it is *more* mechanically correlated with the reported numbers than Loughran-McDonald, not less. Plus: transcript Q&A is full of "Yes." / "Thanks, John." / cross-talk fragments, so an unweighted mean over sentences is dominated by non-substantive utterances. You need length weighting and utterance filtering, and you should expect FinBERT to underperform ΔTone.

More important: the genuinely differentiated measures are the ones you've relegated to a footnote in the crowding section — **question-answer semantic similarity, whether the answer contains a number, answer specificity relative to question specificity, deflection**. Those are cheap to build off the same parsed data, they are not what the vendors sell, and they are the only part of this that plausibly survives 2019–2024. Move them into scope from day one and drop FinBERT to a robustness cell.

---

## Smaller things that will cost you days

- **Guidance midpoint change** as a control: IBES Guidance coverage is spotty and non-random, undefined for non-guiders and metric-switchers, and vanished for hundreds of firms in 2020. As specified this silently drops or biases 40%+ of your sample. Needs an explicit missing-indicator design.
- **Prior-quarter tone as a control *and* ΔTone as a signal family** is near-double-counting; ΔTone residualized on lagged tone is close to mechanical.
- **The [−63,−2] placebo will "fail" even for a clean signal** — tone correlates with the pre-call run-up and 12-1 momentum won't absorb it at sub-industry-relative horizons. You'll over-interpret it. Use within-sector-quarter shuffles (preserving the cross-sectional distribution) instead, and add analysts'-question tone as a should-be-weak control.
- **Cost model.** Corwin-Schultz is noisy and biased for liquid names; use actual quoted spreads for the top 1,500. Flat 5bp impact ignores that this signal fires in clustered earnings windows where spreads widen and crowding peaks. And 400–600% turnover is optimistic once you add universe churn and the 63-day entry/exit; check it, don't assume it. Missing entirely: borrow cost and availability on the bottom quintile of the 501–1500 bucket.
- **Transcript versioning.** Hand-checking 200 calls doesn't fix it. Either reconstruct from the version-history table, or test whether revisions materially move tone; if they do and you can't reconstruct, you have a look-ahead you cannot remove and must disclose as a bound on the result.
- **Timeline.** Two weeks for CIQ transcript assembly, speaker/section parsing, timestamp validation, PIT Compustat, IBES Detail, Hoberg-Phillips, and co-coverage peers is off by a factor of three. Realistically 5–6 weeks of data engineering before any signal exists. Total is 14–16 weeks, not 8.

## What I'd cut

**Europe.** Half of STOXX 600 reports semi-annually, so your event design breaks, the panel halves, and the signal is twice as stale. Multi-language calls, thin Q&A. It will eat three weeks, not one, and produce an uninterpretable answer. Replace it with the **US 1,501–3,000 cap tier**: same pipeline, genuinely different cross-section, and it's where crowding is weakest — so it's both cheaper and more informative about where residual alpha lives.

---

## The sequencing problem, and the cheap version

Your own pitfalls section says: literature public since 2012, a decade of vendor products, expect the effect materially weaker post-2015, near-zero holdout alpha would be "a finding, not a failure." I agree with all of that. Which means **you have written a plan whose most likely outcome you have already predicted, and you've scheduled the deciding test for week 7 of 8.**

Invert it. Two weeks, one analyst:

1. **Two days of vendor and literature triage.** Amenity, Aiera, RavenPack, Bloomberg and Brain all sell transcript sentiment histories. Request a trial file. If a vendor's back-history shows near-zero sector-neutral IR post-2015, you've bought the answer for the cost of a phone call. Also pull the relevant papers beyond Mayew-Venkatachalam — Druz-Wagner-Zeckhauser, Jiang-Lee-Martin-Zhou, and the ML-on-transcripts literature — several already report the decay.
2. **A ten-day spike:** off-the-shelf LM net tone on management Q&A only, ΔTone version, sector-relative, event-time 63-day holding, top 1,500, **2015–2024 only**, no orthogonalization beyond SUE and no robustness grid. One number.

If that spike shows nothing in the recent decade, kill it — no eight-week build recovers a signal that isn't there in the raw data, and every specification choice you'd make to "find" it is the overfitting you're trying to guard against. If it shows something, you've earned the full build, and you now know which period matters.

The one argument for approving the full spend up front is if the real deliverable is the **parsed-transcript data asset and NLP pipeline** — speaker-tagged, section-tagged, timestamp-validated, question-answer paired — because that supports the deflection/specificity measures, topic exposure, supply-chain mentions, and a dozen future projects. That's a defensible infrastructure investment with lexical tone as its first and probably weakest application. If that's the pitch, say so explicitly and budget it as infrastructure. If the pitch is "lexical tone is an alpha signal," do the two-week version first.
